title: Wash, and be clean (2 Kings 5:1–14)
hookLine: the general wanted something grand, and was told to wash in the Jordan

lines: A GREAT MAN, BUT A LEPER.
cards: Horses, chariots, servants, and gifts of silver, gold and fine clothing. Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Aram, has come a long way, and he has come in style.
The text calls him a great man, honored by his king, a mighty man of valor. And then a short phrase undoes all of it: he was a leper. He has a skin disease no rank can cure.
Someone has told him there's a prophet in Israel who could heal him. So the whole procession stops at Elisha's door. And Elisha doesn't come out.

teach.h: GO AND WASH IN THE JORDAN.
teach.b: Instead, Elisha sends a messenger: go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean. No ceremony. No prophet at the door.
Naaman is furious, and the text lets us hear why.

teach.h: I THOUGHT HE WOULD COME OUT.
teach.b: I thought he would surely come out to me, stand there, call on the name of his God, wave his hand over the spot, and heal me. He had pictured the whole scene in advance.
Then the insult of the river itself: are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?
Couldn't I wash in them and be clean? He turns and leaves in a rage. What stops him is not the prophet.
It's his own servants. They call him, my father. If the prophet had asked you to do some great thing, wouldn't you have done it?
"How much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?" A sharp, kind question. Naaman was ready for a quest, a price, a drama worthy of a general.
What he couldn't accept was something ordinary: a plain river, seven dips, no prophet at the bank.

teach.h: LIKE THE FLESH OF A LITTLE CHILD.
teach.b: And yet he goes down to the Jordan, dips himself seven times, just as the man of God said, and his flesh comes back like the flesh of a little child, and he is clean. The cure was there from the first message.
What stood in the way was Naaman's picture of how it should happen. The hard part wasn't the washing. It was getting down off the chariot.

how: Jews read Naaman's healing as part of the book of Kings and as a haftarah alongside the Torah's laws of skin disease, which are read in the book of Leviticus.

o: to have a hand waved over a sore in prayer
to dip in a plain river, as the prophet said
to offer gold and silver for a healing

p: a great man, but a leper

s: Elisha came out and laid hands on Naaman
he sent a messenger; Naaman had expected him to come out.
they asked: if he had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not?
Naaman washed in the rivers of Damascus
he wanted to, but in the end he dipped in the Jordan.

games.q: you're Naaman. the prophet won't even come to the door, and says to wash in the Jordan. what do you do?
o: go home to the rivers of Damascus.
listen to your servants and wash.
games.why: he turns away in a rage, but his servants reason with him. he washes, and his flesh is restored.

practice: Name something you've been stuck on, waiting for a big solution: a tense relationship, a messy room, a project you can't start.

Ask what Naaman's servants asked: if the answer were something grand, would I do it, and what's the plain, ordinary step I keep stepping over? Name it to yourself, and in your mind, step down off the chariot.

wordCard.voice: Wash. The plain instruction a great general almost refused: go down into an ordinary river and dip, as the prophet said. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: wash, and be clean, the servants' words in 2 Kings 5:13.

carryVoice: Your line: getting down off the chariot. Sometimes the ordinary is the whole instruction. Day seven hundred seventy-three, done.

sources.q: How much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?
